name: repo-sast-matrix
description: Per-CLASS, per-LANGUAGE SAST recall for the languages our customers actually write. The neutral SAST benchmark we cite (OWASP Benchmark v1.2) is a JAVA corpus; our ICP writes Go, JavaScript and Python, so the one measurement we could quote said nothing about the code we actually scan. A command injection missed in Python surfaced only because a demo fixture happened to plant one — this exists so the next gap is data instead of luck.
not_a_neutral_benchmark: We wrote these cases, so this is a REGRESSION TEST, not evidence of capability relative to anyone. Quote OWASP Benchmark for a comparative number; quote this only as 'we check these classes and here is the result'.
metric: planted-case recall (per class × language), with FP-control on fixtures/repo/clean

measured.note_on_size: Started at 12 — the minimum to show the gap existed, not a target. Extended to 24 once the harness proved worth having: Go sat at 2 cases against Python's 6, and whole classes (XSS, SSTI, XXE, open redirect, NoSQL injection, TLS-verification-disabled) had no case in any language. Widening found 4 NEW misses beyond the one already known, which is the argument for widening it further. Each case is one small file plus a row here; the expensive part was building the runner, and that is done.

known_miss.why: NOT a ruleset-config gap — unlike the first round, where p/owasp-top-ten recovered 7 of 9 misses. p/python, p/javascript and p/golang catch NONE of these five. They need dataflow/taint analysis: whether `db` is a SQL connection, whether a path is attacker-controlled, whether entity resolution is enabled.
known_miss.architectural_blind_spot: CodeQL is the taint tier that WOULD catch them, and it cannot fire. internal/asset/repository/escalate.go gates it on `isInjectionFinding(f)` — CodeQL only runs when semgrep ALREADY produced an injection finding. When semgrep misses the class entirely there is no finding to escalate from, so the deep tool is gated on the shallow tool having succeeded. For these five classes nothing catches them at any tier. Fixing it means triggering CodeQL on language presence rather than on a prior finding, and paying its runtime — a real trade, and a decision rather than an oversight.

note_on_layout: Cases live under testdata/ because the Go toolchain ignores any directory of that name. Without it `go vet ./...` compiles the planted Go samples — which are deliberately broken code — and fails the build. That is exactly what happened on the first push of this fixture.
